## `Python` and modeling? {.AZ}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
The core of the language does not support:

- ordinary int 
- multi-dimensional arrays
- JIT compilation
- multi-threading
- GPUs
- numerical algorithms


:::

::: {.column .fragment width="70%"}

![](img/StackOverflow.svg)
:::
::::


But `Python` is designed as a **glue language**!

Above features are handled by packages: **NumPy**(C), **SciPy**(C/Fortran/...), **Numba/JAX**(C++/...), and many more!


# <quote>unit-aware coding and plotting</quote>
## a useful physical example: ideal gas {.AZ}
<br>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="15%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}

<span style="font-size:500%">🎈</span>

<span style="font-size:300%">🎈</span>

<span style="font-size:200%">🎈</span>

<span style="font-size:100%">🎈</span>

<span style="font-size:50%">🎈</span>
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

equation of state linking

>  $\rho$: density
> 
>  $p$: pressure
> 
>  $T$: temperature

$$\rho = (p M) / (T R)$$

where

> $M$: molar mass
> 
> $R$: universal gas constant

:::

::::

## Issue: units in code (example: ideal gas density) {.AZ}

$$\rho = (p M) / (T R)$$

. . .

<div class="strike-code">

```{python}
#| code-line-numbers: "1|1-2|1-8|"

import numpy, scipy, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mendeleev

p = 1000                                     # pressure [mbar]
T = numpy.linspace(250, 300)                 # temperature [K]
R = scipy.constants.R                        # gas constant [J/K/mol]
M = (0.78 * 2 * mendeleev.N.atomic_weight +  # molar mass [g/mol]
     0.22 * 2 * mendeleev.O.atomic_weight)

fig, axs = plt.figure(), plt.gca()
axs.plot(T, (p * M) / (R * T))
axs.set(ylabel="density", xlabel="temperature")
```
<div class="fragment strike-code"></div>
</div>
. . .


“_The proper use of comments is to compensate for our failure to express ourself in code ... 
Comments are always failures._” (Robert C. Martin [_Clean Code_, 2009](https://books.google.pl/books/about/Clean_Code.html?id=EpeDEQAAQBAJ&redir_esc=y))


## Issue: units in comments not in code {.AZ} 

The interpreter is not parsing the comments! We always use units on paper, use it in code as well.

- What is the unit of the plotted data?

::: {.fragment}
```{python}
#| echo: false

fig
```
:::

- Reading the code, one needs to go to the definition each time.

::: {.fragment}
```{python}
print(T[0])
``` 
:::

::: {.fragment}
$T$ is time or temperature? 
:::

- No way of enforcing changes in usage upon change of definition.
- After changing the value --- did you change the comment? (We all know the answer...)

## physical units with Pint (example: ideal gas density) {.AZ}

$$\rho = (p M) / (T R)$$

```{python}
#| code-line-numbers: "1|1-2|1-3|1-5|1-6|1-7|1-9|-"

import pint
SI = pint.UnitRegistry()
SI.setup_matplotlib()

pressure = 1000 * SI.mbar
temperatures = numpy.linspace(250, 300) * SI.K
gas_const = scipy.constants.R * SI.J / SI.K / SI.mol
molar_mass = (0.78 * 2 * mendeleev.N.atomic_weight +
              0.22 * 2 * mendeleev.O.atomic_weight) * SI.g / SI.mol

density = (pressure * molar_mass) / (gas_const * temperatures)
plt.plot(temperatures, density)
```

- changed names of variables
- axis labels automatic


## {.AZ}
### Can we ...

::: {.fragment}

- ... change units on plot?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{python}
#| code-line-numbers: "|2-3"

fig, axs = plt.figure(), plt.gca()
axs.xaxis.set_units(SI.degC)
axs.yaxis.set_units(SI.kg / SI.m**3)
axs.plot(temperatures, density)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
- ... change axes labels and still use units?
:::

::: {.fragment}

```{python}
#| code-line-numbers: "|3-4"

fig, axs = plt.figure(), plt.gca()
axs.plot(temperatures, density)
axs.set_xlabel(f"temperature [{axs.xaxis.units:~P}]")
axs.set_ylabel(f"density [{axs.yaxis.units:~P}]");
```
:::

::: {.notes}
to_base_units
pretty formatting
:::

# <quote>dimensional analysis using Pint</quote> {.AZ}

## {.AZ}
### Can we ...

::: {.fragment}

- ... change the units to the wrong ones?
:::

::: {.fragment}

```{python}
#| error: true
plt.gca().yaxis.set_units(SI.J)
plt.plot(pressure)
```
:::



::: {.fragment}

- ... put different quantities on same axis?
:::

::: {.fragment}

```{python}
#| error: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|2-3"
try:
    plt.plot(temperatures)
    plt.plot(temperatures ** 2)
except Exception as e:
    plt.close()
    print(e.__cause__)
```
:::

## {.AZ}
### Can we ...

::: {.fragment}

- ... add Kelvins to Pascals?
:::


::: {.fragment}

```{python}
#| error: true

temperatures + pressure
```

:::

<br>

- Tools for unit testing:

::: {.fragment}

```{python}
((pressure * molar_mass) / (gas_const * temperatures)).check("[density]")
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

```{python}
assert density.check("[density]")
```
:::
## {.AZ}

### Pint: key takeaways

- ⚖️ performs dimensional analysis (unit testing!)
- ⚙️ automates plot axis labelling (and consistency checks)
- 💱 handles SI prefixes and unit conversions
- 🩺 helps in debugging (`print(x)` prints a value with unit)


<br>
<br>

::: {.fragment}
### Pint: key limitations
:::

::: {.fragment .strike}

- ⏱️ incurs performance overhead
:::
::: {.fragment .strike}

- 🔗 no out-of-the-box interoperability with SciPy/Numba
:::


# **JIT compilation using Numba** {.SA}

## Issue: units with `SciPy` and `Numba` {.SA}

Problem with using units with `SciPy`/ `NumPy` packages:
```{python}
#| error: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|1-3|-"

from scipy.optimize import root_scalar

f = lambda T, a, b: a / T + b

root_scalar(
    f=f,
    x0=1 * SI.K,
    args=(2 * SI.K**2, -3 * SI.K)
)
```


::: {.fragment}

<br>

Problem with using just-in-time compilation (`Numba`)
```{python}
#| code-line-numbers: "1|1-5|"
import numba

@numba.jit
def f(a, b, T):
  return a / T + b

print(f"{f(2, -3, 270):.3g}")
```
:::


::: {.fragment}
```{python}
#| error: true

f(2 * SI.K**2, -3 * SI.K, 270 * SI.K)
```

::: 

## Using `Pint` with `SciPy` solvers or with `Numba` JIT compiler {.SA}

(`see Section 4. in the preprint`, based on MSc thesis of Daria Klimaszewska)

<center><b>
  injectable constants-catalogue idiom
</b></center>

<br >

::: {.fragment}

💡 key (physics) principle: dimensionality of physical quantities originates from <b>constants</b> only!    
&nbsp;❶ $\leadsto$ instantiate a constants catalogue at <b>topmost scope</b>, pass to all physics-related functions    
&nbsp;❷ $\leadsto$ use <b>unit-aware</b> constants catalogue for unit testing    
&nbsp;❸ $\leadsto$ use <b>plain-floats</b> constants catalogue elsewhere

:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}

- ✅ no trade-off in <b>code readibility</b> or <b>performance</b> 
- ✅ no trade-off in <b>functionality</b> (e.g., SI prefixes, unit conversions, ...)
- ✅ no trade-off in <b>interoperability</b> with numerical routines or JIT compilers
- 💡 works with <b>any language</b> supporting JIT compilation (e.g., Julia) or templates (e.g., C++)
- ➕ positive side-effect: enforces <b>separation of concerns</b>

:::
